name: Batchbook
idea: Free web production planner for micro-bakeries and cottage food makers: scale formulas, check stock, plan the bake day, print allergen labels.
description: Recipes live as versioned formulas (baker's percentages, yield loss, ingredient densities) so one order list turns into a batch plan, a shopping list and a 'can I make X with what I have?' answer. It also builds the allergen matrix and a printable ingredient/allergen label for the maker's jurisdiction. Aimed at people launching a home or micro bakery who currently run it from spreadsheets; the moat is a curated ingredient-density, unit-conversion and label-rule dataset plus correct scaling math.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel hobby, Supabase Postgres + RLS for recipes/orders; labels rendered to PDF client-side; installable PWA for use in the kitchen.
why_hard_to_copy: Correct recipe scaling (baker's percentages, yield loss, volume-to-weight with ingredient densities) and jurisdiction-specific allergen/label rules are hand-curated data plus edge-case math, not CRUD. The open-source competitor is an Elixir app that non-developers cannot host.

signals.summary: A developer built a production-management tool for his wife's planned micro-bakery because the software he found was either expensive or too generic, then open-sourced it (versioned recipes, lot tracking, allergens, batch planning).

Another developer built local inventory and production software for his dad's small manufacturing business, centred on reorder levels and the question 'can I make X from current stock?', explicitly aiming to beat spreadsheets.

A commenter on the bakery-tool thread says he and his wife looked at buying a small bagel shop in Berlin where the previous owner ran everything in Excel files, and that such software would have helped.

name: Relic
idea: Drag a dBase/FoxPro/Clipper/Paradox data file into the browser, browse it and export CSV/XLSX/SQLite without uploading anything.
description: Small firms still run DOS-era database apps whose data files nobody can open any more, and the people rescuing them hand-write parsers against format specs. Relic reads the common xBase variants (dBase III/IV, FoxPro/VFP, Clipper, memo files, DOS code pages, deleted-record flags) plus fixed-width text exports with a layout wizard, entirely client-side so business data never leaves the machine. Built for the consultant, relative or office manager who inherited the old system; the moat is breadth of format edge cases and a test corpus.
web_delivery: Static Next.js app on Vercel; parsing in a Web Worker with File API, export via client-side CSV/XLSX/SQLite-WASM; Supabase only for optional saved layouts and sample-file feedback.
why_hard_to_copy: Parsing obscure legacy file formats correctly (memo blocks, code pages, packed numerics, variant headers) entirely client-side is exactly the long-tail work generic converters skip; the value compounds with every odd file added to the test corpus.

signals.summary: An Ask HN asking who still keeps a DOS machine running because the business depends on it drew many replies about dBase/Clipper/Paradox/Btrieve systems and ideas for hooking or migrating their .DBF data to modern formats.
A developer's family wholesale business has run on the same 1993 text-UI system for decades; replies list FoxPro, Pick and dBase shops kept alive by one aging maintainer.
A commenter says a .dbf-to-csv converter would have saved him the trouble of writing his own Go parser from the dBase IV spec by trial and error.
A commenter helping a friend's family business had to patch a FoxPro app with hex editors because the original programmer had died.

name: Swiss Desk
idea: Run chess club nights and scholastic tournaments in the browser: Swiss pairings, standings, club ratings, results export, plus a scoresheet-repair tool.
description: Organisers currently juggle Google Forms for sign-up, desktop pairing software and text threads. Swiss Desk handles the roster, QR check-in, Swiss pairing with colour balance, byes and tiebreaks, a local club rating, a public standings link and a results export in the formats rating bodies expect. The builders on HN say matching real-world Swiss pairing rules is harder than it looks, which is the moat.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel, Supabase Postgres with Realtime for live standings; pairing engine in TypeScript runs client-side and is unit-tested against known tournaments.
why_hard_to_copy: Swiss pairing rules (transpositions, colour alternation, floaters, forfeits, tiebreaks) and rating-report file formats are correctness-critical domain logic that a generic bracket builder gets wrong; one HN builder calls Swiss pairings 'more nuanced than they look'.

signals.summary: A new local chess club founder searched for software to manage members, games and a local club rating, found only paid options, and built an open-source club manager himself.

A parent who volunteers at his kid's tournaments saw the workflow split across Google Forms, payment apps, SwissSys/WinTD pairings and email/text, and is building a unified tool; says matching existing Swiss pairing workflows is the hard part.

A parent and his son keep mistyping moves when copying score sheets, and PGN parsers discard everything after the first error, so he built a viewer that highlights the error and keeps the remaining moves.

name: Fixture Glue
idea: Paste or upload a league's fixture list and get a subscribable calendar feed plus a weekly 'who can play?' poll for the team.
description: Amateur players and sports parents deal with leagues that each publish fixtures differently (web tables, PDFs, CSVs, printed sheets) and team chats that live elsewhere. Fixture Glue parses the common layouts client-side, normalises dates, times, venues and time zones, outputs a webcal feed that updates when a game moves, and gives the captain a one-click availability poll. The moat is a growing library of league-format parsers plus change detection.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; PDF text extraction with pdf.js and table heuristics run in the browser; ICS feed served from a Vercel route backed by Supabase; poll links need no login.
why_hard_to_copy: The hard part is a messy-schedule parser library (odd date formats, multi-column PDFs, bye weeks, rescheduled games) and diffing updates, which accumulates league by league and is not a weekend job.

signals.summary: A commenter who plays on several teams and leagues says every league delivers fixtures its own way and every team chats elsewhere; he wants software that glues fixtures to a weekly 'who is playing' poll, but the market is too fragmented for conventional products.

name: Sideline Story

name: Slotbook
idea: Free, ad-free volunteer slot sign-ups for PTAs, clubs and congregations with recurring shifts, reminders and service-hour totals.
description: School and club coordinators fight sign-up tools that charge to remove ads and lose track of past events, or fall back to chat threads. Slotbook handles roles, slot caps, recurring shifts, swap requests, email reminders and per-volunteer hour totals, with one link and no volunteer accounts. name: Org Memory
idea: A handover binder for small volunteer-run organisations: policy review dates, officer terms, building maintenance records and renewals, with reminders and an audit log.
description: Small charities, churches and clubs lose records when the volunteer treasurer or retired admin leaves, and governance tools are priced for large boards. Org Memory keeps officer terms, policy review cycles, insurance and licence renewals, building inspections and invoices in one place, nudges the chair when a term or review is due, auto-fills meeting agendas and exports a handover pack. The moat is a curated, jurisdiction-specific governance and maintenance calendar (UK charity cycles first), not the file store.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; Supabase Postgres with RLS and Storage for photos/PDFs (small files), email reminders via a free-tier email API on a scheduled function.
why_hard_to_copy: The value is hand-curated governance calendars, policy templates and building-maintenance schedules by jurisdiction and building type, kept current by someone who knows the sector; a generic CRUD tracker lacks that.

name: Quorum
idea: Free-to-start voting and quorum tracking for HOAs, clubs and congregations, with ranked-choice tallying, proxies and a paper-ballot fallback.
description: Volunteer board members run an election once a year, worry that results can be challenged, and fear that members who do not use email get left out. Quorum handles member lists, one-person-one-ballot links, proxy and paper-ballot entry, live quorum tracking, several tally methods and a tamper-evident audit log. The moat is correct tally and quorum rules (single transferable vote, cumulative voting, proxy limits) and trust-building audit trails.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; Supabase with RLS for ballots and a hash-chained audit table; ballot links by email through a free-tier email API (volume-limited).
why_hard_to_copy: Tally algorithms (STV, cumulative, weighted votes), proxy/quorum rule engines, paper-ballot reconciliation and verifiable audit trails are correctness-critical and trust-critical, unlike a poll widget.

name: Porch Board
idea: Email-first community board for neighbourhood associations and small clubs: members get a digest and can post by email or web, admins moderate in one queue.
description: Groups leaving Facebook say older members will not learn Slack or forums, CC-list emails are a mess, and forum software with email notifications 'dies fast'. why_hard_to_copy: Weak: any developer can build a forum. Defensibility would come only from email-first threading/digest design that works for 70+ members and group-by-group adoption, i.e. small-niche network effects.

name: Table Fill

description: Hosts of recurring meetups say they cannot predict attendance and many games break at the wrong player count, and the leading platform has become expensive for organisers. Table Fill shows an expected-turnout range from each group's RSVP history, auto-promotes waitlisted people and suggests games from a shared library that work for the confirmed head-count, with a fallback pick if the count drops. name: Seat Solver
idea: Paste a messy guest list and get it cleaned, grouped into households and seated automatically with keep-together and keep-apart rules.
description: People planning a wedding or party hand-assemble guest lists from texts, photos of address books and spreadsheets, then try to seat guests by trial and error. Seat Solver imports pasted lists and CSVs, merges duplicates, groups households, takes simple rules (sit with, keep apart, table sizes) and solves a seating plan you can drag to adjust and print. The moat is the optimisation (an NP-complete seating problem needing a good heuristic) plus robust list cleaning.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; solver runs client-side in a Web Worker; Supabase only for saved plans; print-to-PDF layout.
why_hard_to_copy: Seating is an NP-complete constraint problem; a solid heuristic (simulated annealing with weighted preferences) plus tolerant guest-list parsing is more than a drag-and-drop canvas.

signals.summary: A commenter says he built a small tool with a simple constraint solver to decide the seating chart for his own small wedding, and that it left him confident in the result.

A commenter planning a wedding describes assembling the guest list from texts, photos of his father's address book and Excel files, and says an AI agent could not do such messy data and website tasks reliably.

name: Camp Radar
idea: A hand-curated calendar of when local summer camp and class registrations open, with reminders ahead of each opening day.
description: Parents miss registration windows and end up taking whatever spots are left, because dates are scattered across town recreation pages and individual camp sites (resident-first windows, late-fee cutoffs and aid deadlines vary). Camp Radar starts with one metro area, hand-collects each provider's opening, resident-priority, late-fee and aid dates, and emails or exports ICS reminders per family. The moat is the curated dataset kept current, not the reminder code.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; Supabase table of providers/dates edited by an admin page; ICS export and email reminders from a scheduled function.
why_hard_to_copy: The defensible part is a hand-collected, locally verified registration-date dataset (and parent corrections), which takes sustained manual work per metro area.

name: Routine Boards
idea: Free web builder for printable and on-screen visual schedules and first-then boards for children who are non-verbal or autistic.
description: Parents of children who rely on picture schedules describe laminated cards and velcro boards as hard to manage and impossible to take along. Routine Boards lets caregivers build a day schedule or first-then board from an open pictogram library or their own photos, print it at true card sizes and use the same board full-screen on any tablet. The moat is a licensed, well-organised symbol set and print layouts, plus offline use.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel; boards stored in Supabase with photos kept small or local; offline caching with a service worker; print CSS for card sizes.
why_hard_to_copy: Curation and correct licensing of an open pictogram set, plus print layouts matched to real laminate/velcro card sizes and offline reliability, are more careful than a generic to-do board. Weak against apps from the same builder.

signals.summary: A solo developer and father of three, two with severe disabilities, says visual schedules (laminated cards, velcro boards) are a lifeline for non-verbal children but a nightmare to manage and do not leave the house, so he built an app for them.

name: Gran Screen
idea: A caregiver-managed big-button home page for older relatives: only the links, audiobooks, radio, video-call and photos you choose, installable from the browser.
description: Adult children report that parents struggle with logins, two-factor flows and modern sites, and that off-the-shelf senior tablets or kiosk apps are native and costly. Gran Screen is a PWA home page with large tiles for the few sites and media the family chooses, remotely edited by a caregiver, with ad-free simple games and a daily 'I am fine' tap. It cannot lock down a device like a native kiosk app; the plan is to be the lightest option that works on any tablet already in the house.
web_delivery: Installable PWA on Vercel; Supabase stores each household's tile list and caregiver permissions; media is links/streams only, no hosting of audio or video.
why_hard_to_copy: Weak: simple to rebuild. Differentiation comes from caregiver-side remote control plus carefully usability-tested defaults for 80+ users, which takes real testing with seniors rather than code.

signals.summary: A founder whose SaaS has been used by people over 65 for ten years asks how to simplify sign-in because users forget the address and which email and password they used and find Google sign-in confusing.

name: Open When
idea: A family binder that tells loved ones where everything is and what to do with each online account after you die or are incapacitated, without storing passwords.
description: People worry about what a spouse would face with email, photo storage, subscriptions and documents after a death, and a password manager alone does not explain what to do. Open When keeps an inventory of accounts by provider with the exact memorialise/close/transfer steps, who the family contact is and where documents live, encrypted in the browser and released to named people only on a check-in lapse or manual trigger. The moat is a curated, regularly updated per-provider procedures dataset plus careful client-side encryption.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; client-side encryption (Web Crypto) before data reaches Supabase; scheduled function sends a check-in email and releases a sealed link to trusted contacts if unanswered.
why_hard_to_copy: The provider-by-provider procedures dataset (Apple, Google, Meta, banks' notification steps etc.) must be researched and kept current, and zero-knowledge encryption plus a safe release flow is easy to get wrong.

signals.summary: An Ask HN asks how people manage their digital legacy, worrying about what his wife would face with accounts, old photos and documents after his death beyond handing over a password manager.

A student launched Seal, an iOS app for encrypted letters and passwords that open for family after a long inactivity countdown; commenters questioned device loss, Apple dependency and the inactivity trigger, and one asked why it is not a client-side web app.

name: Table Captions
idea: A shared live-captions page for small gatherings: one phone listens, everyone else reads the text on their own screen.
description: Hearing-aid users say restaurants, parties and group conversations remain hard even with aids, and people build captioning tools for hard-of-hearing family members. Table Captions turns any phone browser into the microphone and shows large, speaker-labelled text on any screen via a join code, aimed at church groups, clubs, family dinners and small meetings. It relies on the browser's built-in speech recognition for the free core.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel; Web Speech API in the speaker's browser; Supabase Realtime broadcasts text to joined viewers; no audio is stored or uploaded to our servers.
why_hard_to_copy: Weak. A vibe coder can wire the Web Speech API in a weekend; the only defensible parts are reliable multi-device sync, readable caption styling for hearing loss and group-friendly speaker labelling.

name: Plug-In Solar Rulebook
idea: Enter your country or US state and address: see whether plug-in (balcony) solar is allowed, the wattage cap, what to register, which devices qualify, and a realistic yield estimate.
description: Plug-in solar became legal or semi-legal in the UK, several US states and elsewhere during 2026, and every thread shows confusion: which certification applies, how many panels per circuit, what renters can do, what a US 120 V split-phase home means. The tool combines a hand-maintained rules table (caps, registration steps, certification such as UL 3700, circuit and socket limits, renter notes) with a free-data yield and payback estimate for the roof or balcony direction. The moat is the curated, constantly changing regulatory dataset plus honest uncertainty ranges, which generic solar calculators and one-country tools lack.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; rules stored as versioned rows in Supabase (with source links and last-verified dates); yield estimate calls a free public solar-irradiance API from a Vercel route with caching; static pages per country/state for search traffic.
why_hard_to_copy: A hand-curated, dated rules dataset across jurisdictions that changed repeatedly in 2026, plus shading/orientation modelling and circuit-safety checks, needs domain research and upkeep that a quick vibe-coded calculator will not have.

signals.summary: A 264-point thread on plug-in solar panels shows constant confusion about legality, split-phase US wiring, utility approval, circuit limits and who can install what.

Thread on UK households being free to install plug-in balcony solar: commenters ask where this stands in the US, whether the meter will show it, and one lists three headaches for US buyers (device certification that barely exists yet, hard-to-source panels, state-by-state rules).
